content:
**Quick answer:** To exercise with arthritis without making pain worse, start gently, choose manageable activities, move within a comfortable range and increase activity gradually. Some temporary discomfort can occur, but sharp, severe, unusual or persistent pain is a reason to stop and reassess. A physiotherapist can help tailor exercise if you are unsure.

## The balance you are aiming for

Exercising safely with arthritis usually means finding the right balance between movement and recovery. Appropriate exercise can support muscle strength, mobility, balance, physical function and confidence, and for people with osteoarthritis, NICE recommends therapeutic exercise tailored to the individual. But exercise does not cure arthritis or reverse joint changes, and you do not need to push through severe pain to benefit from movement.

What works for one person may not work for another, and exercise should not feel like punishment.

## Does pain during exercise mean damage?

Not necessarily. Pain and joint damage are not the same thing in every situation, and joints that are already painful or stiff, plus muscles that have not been used much, can make symptoms more noticeable when activity increases. Pain after exercise needs context: how severe it is, whether it feels familiar, whether it is sharp or unusual, whether movement becomes difficult, whether there is new swelling, and how long symptoms last afterwards.

There is no universal pain number that is right for everyone. Useful questions during exercise include: does this feel manageable? Is the movement controlled? Am I changing how I move because of pain? Are my symptoms escalating? How do I feel after I stop, and am I recovering reasonably afterwards?

> **Pain that means stop**
>
> Stop exercising for sharp pain, severe pain, unusual pain, pain that is suddenly much worse, pain with sudden significant swelling, pain with an inability to bear weight, or persistent and concerning pain after you stop. Do not follow a "no pain, no gain" approach.

## How to start

Starting slowly matters because a common mistake is doing too much on a motivated good day. A steadier pattern of manageable activity, recovery, repetition and gradual increases is more practical than occasional bursts of demanding activity. A gentle warm-up, such as walking slowly or easy versions of the planned exercise, can help before more active sessions.

1. Choose one manageable activity: a short walk, gentle mobility movement, seated exercise, light strengthening, cycling, swimming or water-based activity.
2. Keep the first session manageable. You do not need to prove what you can do on the first day.
3. Notice your response: during the activity, shortly afterwards, later in the day and the following morning.
4. Build gradually rather than making a large jump if the activity feels manageable.
5. Adapt when needed. Your routine does not need to look identical every day.

## Exercise types, and no gym required

No single type of exercise is automatically best for everyone. Mobility work maintains comfortable movement; strengthening supports the muscles around your joints; aerobic activity such as walking, cycling or swimming supports fitness; balance and flexibility work support stability and comfortable range; water exercise and seated exercise offer supported and accessible options.

You do not need an expensive gym membership or specialist equipment to begin moving more. Walking, sit-to-stand movements, gentle mobility exercises, supported standing exercises and simple strengthening recommended by a physiotherapist all work at home. For strengthening, bodyweight movements, resistance bands and light resistance are enough to begin.

If you stretch, keep it controlled: avoid bouncing, avoid forcing the joint, do not push into sharp pain and do not chase the largest possible range. Some people find stretching more comfortable after warming up.

## When exercise makes pain worse

First, reduce or stop the activity that is aggravating your symptoms. Then consider what changed: did you exercise for longer than usual, increase resistance, try a new activity, skip breaks, combine several demanding activities, or start on an already difficult arthritis day? Is this pain different from your normal symptoms?

Once symptoms have settled, you may be able to return at a lower level. One difficult session does not mean exercise is unsuitable for you; it may mean the amount, intensity, duration or type needs adjusting. When progressing, change one factor at a time so you can understand how your body responds. If pain is severe, persistent, unusual or keeps happening despite adjustments, seek professional advice.

## Pacing across the day and week

Pacing means balancing activity with recovery and choosing a level you can repeat comfortably. If symptoms usually increase substantially after a longer activity, begin with a shorter manageable period and build from there. Activity can also be spread across the day: gentle mobility in the morning, a short walk at midday, household tasks in the afternoon, rest or gentle movement in the evening.

Not every type of exercise needs to happen every day. A routine can include active days, strengthening days, gentle movement, normal daily activity and recovery. Rest is useful, particularly during difficult periods, but complete inactivity for long periods can contribute to stiffness and reduced strength.

## Flares, fatigue, mornings and swollen joints

During a flare-up, reduce intensity, shorten the session, choose gentler movement, take more breaks or temporarily avoid an activity that clearly aggravates symptoms. A flare does not necessarily mean complete bed rest, but severe, unusual or rapidly worsening symptoms should be medically assessed.

Fatigue can make exercise particularly difficult; on lower-energy days, reduce the duration, intensity or number of exercises rather than abandoning activity altogether. If you are particularly stiff in the morning, begin with gentle joint movement and normal light activity, then exercise more fully later.

If a joint is significantly more swollen, hot or painful than usual, do not force it through your normal programme. Reduce demanding activity and consider seeking medical advice, particularly if the change is sudden or unexplained; a hot, very painful and suddenly swollen joint can need urgent assessment.

And on painkillers: medication decisions should be discussed with a GP or pharmacist. Do not start, stop, increase or change medication specifically to enable exercise without appropriate medical advice.

## Common mistakes

- Doing too much on good days. Increase gradually instead.
- Stopping all movement because of pain. Some symptoms require rest or assessment, but avoiding all movement for prolonged periods has drawbacks too.
- Trying to push through severe pain. Pain is not a challenge you need to defeat.
- Comparing yourself with other people. Someone else's routine tells you very little about what is appropriate for you.
- Increasing too many things at once. Progress one aspect gradually where possible.
- Expecting immediate results. Building strength, confidence and a sustainable routine takes time.

## When to stop and seek advice

A physiotherapist can help if you do not know where to start, you are worried about damaging your joints, exercise repeatedly makes symptoms worse, your walking or balance has changed, or you are returning to activity after a difficult period.

Stop and seek medical advice if exercise repeatedly causes substantial worsening, pain is becoming more severe, a joint is increasingly swollen, you have new symptoms, your mobility has changed significantly, or you repeatedly struggle to bear weight. Seek urgent help for sudden severe pain, sudden swelling, a hot and very painful joint, signs of infection or fever, or sudden inability to bear weight. Call emergency services for chest pain, severe breathing difficulty or sudden serious neurological symptoms.

## Key takeaways

- Exercise can support strength, mobility and confidence when adapted safely; it does not cure or reverse arthritis.
- Start gently, choose movements that suit your ability, and change one part of your routine at a time when progressing.
- Some discomfort does not automatically mean joint damage, but sharp, severe, unusual or persistent pain should not be ignored.
- Walking, cycling, swimming, strengthening and seated activity may all be options, and you do not need a gym.
- Fatigue is a valid reason to adjust your routine, and exercise may need adapting during a flare-up.

## Frequently asked questions

### Should I exercise if my joints hurt?

It depends on the pain and your condition. Gentle movement may still be appropriate when joints feel mildly uncomfortable or stiff, but severe, sharp, unusual or rapidly worsening pain should not be pushed through.

### How do I know if I have exercised too much?

A substantial increase in pain, stiffness, swelling, fatigue or difficulty with normal activities afterwards may indicate the session was more than you could comfortably manage.

### How quickly should I increase exercise?

Increase gradually rather than making large jumps. Consider changing one factor at a time, such as duration or resistance, and notice how your body responds.

### When should I see a physiotherapist about arthritis exercise?

Consider physiotherapy if you are unsure where to start, exercise repeatedly worsens symptoms, your mobility or balance has changed, or you need an exercise programme adapted to your condition.

## A gentle next step

Exercising without making pain worse is not about finding the hardest workout you can tolerate. It is about finding movement that feels manageable, adapting when symptoms change and gradually building confidence. Some days involve more activity and others need a gentler approach; what matters is a routine that works with your body rather than against it. If you are unsure, a physiotherapist can help tailor exercise to you. You can also explore practical arthritis information and support from Living With Arthritis.
